title: The Rivers and the Sea
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: Once upon a time all the Rivers combined to protest against the action of the Sea in making their waters salt. "When we come to you," said they to the Sea, "we are sweet and drinkable: but when once we have mingled with you, our waters become as briny and unpalatable as your own." The Sea replied shortly, "Keep away from me and you'll remain sweet."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did all the Rivers combine to do?
options: Protest against the Sea's action of making their waters salt
Race each other to the ocean
Ask the Sea for more water

questions.prompt: According to the Rivers, what are they like when they come to the Sea?
According to the Rivers, what happens to their waters once they have mingled with the Sea?
options: They become as briny and unpalatable as the Sea's own water

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Sea reply to the Rivers' complaint?
options: "Keep away from me and you'll remain sweet"
"I will try to change my ways"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, in what manner did the Sea reply?
As the passage uses it, what does "unpalatable" mean in "as briny and unpalatable as your own"?
Based on the passage, what is the logical flaw in the Rivers' complaint against the Sea?
options: They blame the Sea for a change that only happens because they choose to join it
They have never actually tasted the Sea's water themselves
They are complaining about a problem that does not really exist
They want the Sea to become sweeter than they are

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: You cannot fairly blame another for an effect that only comes from choosing to join them
The Sea is more powerful than any river could ever be
Rivers should never flow into the sea at all
Salt water is always more valuable than fresh water

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who protests against the Sea?
options: The fish living in the Sea

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what exactly are the Rivers protesting the Sea for doing?
According to the passage, what word describes what happens between the Rivers' water and the Sea's water?
As the passage uses it, what does "mingled" mean in "once we have mingled with you"?
Based on the passage, what is the Sea suggesting the Rivers could do to stay sweet?
options: Never flow into the Sea in the first place
Ask the Sea to filter out its own salt
Flow faster so the salt cannot mix in
Combine into a single, larger river

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: The Rivers blame the Sea for their waters turning salty, and the Sea replies that avoiding it is the only solution
The Sea apologizes to the Rivers and promises to stop mixing with them
The Rivers agree that salt water tastes better than sweet water
The Sea threatens to dry up the Rivers unless they stop protesting
